forces: Trumpets, horns, oboes, bassoon, strings and continuo
performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Major Michelle Rakers, conductor
intro: The Marine Chamber Orchestra ends its Water Music programme with this twenty-four-bar minuet in D major from Suite No. 2, HWV 349. The orchestra plays both strains with their repeats and then plays the whole minuet again.

sections.label: A · Eight-bar strain in D major
sections.mNote: Repeated notes above a moving bass in D major.

sections.label: B · Sixteen-bar strain
sections.mNote: The brass rest for the first three bars.

sections.label: A′ · First strain returns
sections.mNote: The opening eight bars, now played once.

sections.label: B′ · Sixteen-bar strain returns
sections.mNote: The sixteen-bar strain returns once to close the programme.

cues.title: Opening on repeated F♯
cues.text: The melody begins by repeating F♯, three crotchets in a bar. Below it, the bass steps through D major. The upper parts have short runs and dotted rhythms over a steady three-beat pulse.
cues.evidence: Samuel Arnold’s full score, The Celebrated Water-musick (1788), p. 52, the D major movement headed Coro: opening repeated F♯ in first oboe and violin, with moving bass. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(28_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second strain, brass resting
cues.text: The second strain begins with the brass resting. Oboes and strings play three bars on their own before trumpets and horns join them. The bass moves without a break as the brass enter.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 53; Minuet, bars 9–12 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. This describes the written scoring; the performing edition and distribution of the repeats are uncredited.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Arnold’s full score, London, 1788
cues.text: In London in 1788, seventy-one years after the royal river party, Samuel Arnold published Water Music in full score. The D major minuet comes last in his edition. Beneath its final chord is the word Finis.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 52–53, headed Coro and ending FINIS. Publication history and the 1717 river party: Robert King’s note, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66967

cues.title: Return of the minuet
cues.text: The orchestra returns to the beginning and plays the two strains once each, without repeats. The repeated F♯s come back, and the longer second strain closes on a D major chord.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 52–53: eight-bar and sixteen-bar strains, with a D major close. The established sections identify this final traversal without the internal repeats.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Royal barge party, 17 July 1717
cues.text: On 17 July 1717 George I travelled up the Thames to Chelsea, with fifty players on a barge beside his. Friedrich Bonet, the Prussian resident, reported to Berlin that neither the Prince nor the Princess of Wales took part. In November the king, who had quarrelled with his son, ejected him from the palace.
cues.evidence: Bonet to Berlin, 30 July 1717 (New Style), in the Handel Reference Database: https://web.stanford.edu/~ichriss/HRD/1717.htm. The 1717 rift and the November ejection: Robert King’s note for Hyperion CDA66967, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66967

transitions.title: Moving bass beneath held chords
transitions.from: A · Eight-bar strain in D major
transitions.how: The upper parts hold D major while the bass outlines the chord in crotchets, D–F♯–A. After the repeat of the first strain, Handel begins the longer second strain with oboes, strings and bass. Trumpets and horns rest for three bars, then rejoin.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 52–53; Minuet, bars 8–12 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. The first strain’s held upper chord has a moving bass; the next three bars rest the brass.

transitions.title: The D major dance returns
transitions.how: The sixteen-bar strain ends on a held D major chord with D in the bass. The orchestra goes back to the opening repeated F♯ notes and the three-beat bass. On this final pass each strain is played once.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 52–53: final D major chord and opening minuet. The established section boundary marks the complete dance’s return.

transitions.title: From the first strain to the second
transitions.how: The first strain ends with the upper parts holding D major over the moving bass. The second strain follows directly, without a repeat of the first. In its first three bars the trumpets and horns rest. The full scoring then returns, and the bass reaches D at the close.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 52–53; Minuet, bars 8–24 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. The existing sections identify the last traversal of both strains.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor)
fields.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. The video’s closing frames show the whole orchestra standing; the ensemble’s harpsichord, bassoon and trumpet are visible in the other movements’ videos, and no frame shows horns or oboes. Which sections play in each statement is not established: an independent look at the official video reports upper-string players resting at about 1:05, where the printed score gives them notes, so the recording is not assumed to follow the printed parts. No orchestra view is authored for this movement for that reason.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (13 of the three suites) and the strains heard (a first strain of 8 bars and a second of 16, each played twice) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text. The recording then plays all 24 bars once more without repeats, which that edition does not print; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
fields.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962) prints 24 bars with a repeat sign after bar 8 and after bar 24 and no da capo; the second statement follows from the measured pauses (about 54 s for 24 bars at the first statement’s pace) and is a feature of this performance. Commons and the candidate list place this movement fifth in the suite; the edition numbers it third (13), and Arnold’s 1788 score prints it last, headed Coro.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Commons gives performance_date 2017-01-29; the programme prints Sunday, January 29, 2017 at 2:00 P.M.; the official video description repeats the date. This Minuet is the last item of the programme. The Commons composition_date field, 1717-07-17, is the date of the documented first performance on the Thames, not a composition date.

fields.value: Rachel M. Schlesinger Concert Hall and Arts Center, Northern Virginia Community College, Alexandria Campus, Alexandria, Virginia, United States

fields.label: Label
fields.note: No record label is identified. The source is an official concert video on the Marine Band’s YouTube channel; the channel is not treated as a label, and no commercial release was found.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or mastering engineer is identified. The Commons file history shows the batch upload by the user Mysterymanblue (pattypan), which is an uploader credit, not an engineering credit.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is documented. The YouTube publication date (30 April 2018) and the Commons upload date (28 June 2021) are not session or transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Opus audio file (48 kHz, two channels, encoder Lavf58.29.100) listed on Commons with the Marine Band’s YouTube playlist as its source; Commons supplies an MP3 access derivative. The file keeps the audience’s applause after the last chord.
fields.note: The file’s own metadata documents the Opus format and encoder. That the audio was taken from the official video’s sound track is inferred from the source field and from the matching title and duration (195 s); the processing chain is not described. That the closing half-minute is applause is inferred from its sound and from the standing players and audience silhouettes in the video’s last frames.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Handel (died 1759): the composition is in the public domain.
fields.note: Commons tags the composition PD-old-auto-expired (death year 1759). The performing edition is not identified; editorial copyright in a modern edition, if one was used, is separate from the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Commons tags the performance and recording PD-USGov-Military-Marines: a work of a United States Marine or employee made as part of official duties, public domain as a work of the U.S. federal government.
fields.note: This is a U.S.-jurisdiction statement, not a claim of worldwide status. The programme carries a general notice that a performance may contain third-party material and should not be assumed to be public domain; no third-party material is identified in this performance of a composition from before 1759, but the notice is recorded here. The official Marine Band YouTube channel published the source video.

composer.epithet: Composer who filled London theatres with Italian opera and later put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg had a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant, and Prince Ruspoli provided him with singers and instrumentalists to write for. In the Dixit Dominus of 1707, a setting of a Latin psalm, five choral parts move at speed, then some voices hold dissonant notes while the others move underneath. He wrote chamber cantatas for a single singer. In Corelli’s Rome he learned to write for violin alongside the voice.
